question: Can one shared checkpoint train a large, architecture-agnostic pool of prefix-truncated neural submodels across depth, width, heads, blocks, and embeddings, then deliver accurate budget-adaptive inference without material search, storage, training, or inference overhead?

key_findings.claim: SortedNet's genuine scalable mechanism is prefix sharing plus stochastic coverage, but its pool size is not its per-update computation: a sampled prefix submodel, or a related set under the summation variant, receives the loss at each iteration.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 1 forms each submodel by intersecting parameter prefixes tied to index 1 along sampled architectural dimensions. The stochastic objective updates one selected submodel; the stochastic-summation alternative adds selected related submodels. A common classifier and one checkpoint reduce storage, while the sampling distribution and supported prefix indices define which configurations actually train.

anchors.section: 3.1 A Generalized and Scalable View, Equation 1

key_findings.claim: The abstract's statement that all 160 trained submodels achieve at least 96% of the original model's performance is contradicted by Figure 2 and by the main text's weaker 'up to 96%' statement.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 2a reports a 95.45-accuracy largest MobileNetV2 reference, but numerous small depth-width cells recover far below 96%; the smallest is approximately 9.99 accuracy and 11% recovery, and many cells lie in roughly the 20%-50% range. Section 4.1 instead says the method preserved 'up to 96%' across both dimensions and up to 99% when sorting width alone. 'At least' and 'up to' reverse the quantifier and cannot both describe the displayed 160-model grid.

key_findings.claim: The paper demonstrates search-free prefix extraction, not search-free choice of an accurate budgeted architecture.
key_findings.evidence: Section 3.1 says importance sorting lets the best submodel for a budget be selected without search. Yet Section 4.2 builds Figure 2b only after evaluating the preceding 160-model grid, selecting widths above 60% and depths above 13 blocks, and retraining that subset. Its proposed automatic procedure likewise evaluates every submodel, sorts performance, and threshold-filters the pool. Thus the index rule makes extraction deterministic after a configuration is chosen, while the reported configuration-selection procedure still performs pool-wide empirical evaluation.

anchors.section: 4.2 Can we find the best sub-models using SortedNet?

key_findings.claim: The stated negligible-training-overhead claim is not supported by the disclosed MobileNet schedule or by an end-to-end cost comparison.
key_findings.evidence: Table 7 specifies 60 multiplied by the number of models as the MobileNetV2 epoch schedule, one seed (4242), and eight V100 GPUs; for the 160-model experiment that notation implies 9,600 epochs of sampled training exposure. The only timing study records five individual epochs, drops the first, and compares 49.7 +/- 2.06 seconds for SortedNet with 292.7 +/- 3.17 for LCS-p; multiplying SortedNet by four gives 198.8 seconds for matched update significance. This is a useful local per-epoch result, but it neither compares with one ordinary MobileNet training run nor reports time-to-target accuracy, total accelerator-hours, or energy.

anchors.section: C.3 Table 7 and C.4 training-time protocol

key_findings.claim: The convergence analysis does not establish that a jointly trained SortedNet submodel stays close to an independently trained model.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix B first derives the operative recurrence ||theta_(t+1)-phi_(t+1)|| <= (1+eta L)||theta_t-phi_t|| + eta C, where C bounds inherent cross-objective gradient differences. It then declares C practically zero under identical data, initialization, and hyperparameters. A SortedNet prefix is not identically optimized: its shared parameters also receive gradients when other, usually larger, submodels are sampled, so C represents the central interaction rather than a negligible nuisance. Even after setting C=0, 1+eta L exceeds one and supplies an expansive upper bound, not contraction or convergence; exact same initialization and gradients would merely make equality trivial.

anchors.section: B.5 Negligible C under Identical Training Conditions

key_findings.claim: Equation 3 is not a valid performance bound for trained networks as written.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix B Taylor-expands the model output f(x;theta), then imposes the 'optimum condition' gradient_theta f(x;theta*)=0. Optimization makes a training-loss gradient stationary, not each input-conditioned model output. The derivation also changes from assumptions on loss gradients to output gradients, uses an approximation without a controlled remainder, and writes a one-sided Delta f inequality without bounding absolute deviation. Consequently the claimed quadratic output guarantee does not follow from the paper's assumptions.

key_findings.claim: SortedNet improves average RoBERTa intermediate-layer utility substantially, but it does not preserve the full model and the broad superiority claim is not uniform across compression levels.
key_findings.evidence: Table 3 gives an average of 76.67 for Sorted-RoBERTa versus 52.86 for untrained truncations, an absolute gain of 23.81 points, while its 12-layer model scores 84.16 versus 86.13 for the baseline. In Table 2, SortedNet-IN averages 84.55 versus 84.10 for slimmable NS and 82.76 for LCS-p, only a 0.45-point lead over NS; at 25% width it scores 75.10 below LCS-p's 76.17. Under BatchNorm, SortedNet's mean advantage is driven partly by avoiding extreme small-width failures, yet it still loses individual 75% and 25% comparisons to LCS-p. The evidence supports competitive averages, not dominance at every budget.

key_findings.claim: The LLaMA experiment establishes a task-specific speed-quality menu, not output-preserving self-speculative decoding or general LLM acceleration.
key_findings.evidence: On one fine-tuned LLaMA-13B GSM8K setting, stochastic-loss full decoding is 96.41 ms/token at 23.95 accuracy. Confidence exit reaches 2.09x but falls to 20.69; Sorted self-speculation reaches 2.01x at 23.27 for layers 12:40 and 1.98x at 24.33 for layers 12:24. Because accuracy differs from full decoding, these rows do not show output identity. The summation-loss model has a different full reference (86.10 ms/token, 25.24 accuracy), and no uncertainty, prompt/output protocol, seed, or LLaMA hyperparameter block is supplied.

key_findings.claim: The gradient-accumulation ablation confounds accumulation with total data exposure and does not justify faster convergence from stochasticity.
key_findings.evidence: Table 5 fixes 200 optimizer updates but raises epochs from 200 to 800 as accumulation rises from 1 to 4, with average accuracy rising from 80.85 to 83.95. Table 6 instead fixes 200 epochs, causing update counts to fall from 200 to 50 while averages become 80.85, 80.75, 81.63, and 82.19. The claimed approximately 2% drop for accumulation 2 comes from comparing 82.53 across 400 epochs with 80.75 across 200 epochs, not from a controlled accumulation-only contrast. More epochs, examples, effective batch, and update count vary across comparisons.

key_findings.claim: The complex-dimension BERT study reveals a major small-submodel deficit that weakens the architecture-general claim.
key_findings.evidence: Across five seeds, jointly sorted BERT-base averages 66.42 after approximately 1.5 base plus 1.5 large epochs and 70.03 after approximately 3 plus 3, versus 81.07 for independently fine-tuned BERT-base. Sorted BERT-large reaches 81.98 and 83.26 versus 83.11 independently. The authors acknowledge that base remains about ten points behind and defer SortedNet pretraining; the result supports shared large-model viability but not uniformly successful simultaneous width/depth/head extraction.

key_findings.claim: The paper has no public artifact sufficient to reproduce its results, and its hyperparameter appendix is incomplete despite claiming coverage of all experiments.
key_findings.evidence: The manuscript is labeled a preprint under review and supplies no code, repository, checkpoint, data, environment, or raw-result URL anywhere in its 20 pages. Table 7 covers BERT/RoBERTa, MobileNetV2, and cPreResNet20 but omits the LLaMA-13B/GSM8K optimizer, learning rate, epochs, seed, decoding configuration, hardware, and preprocessing. Exact-title, paper-ID, and author-method repository searches found no official public implementation as of 2026-08-24, preventing independent reproduction of the core 160-model and LLaMA claims.

method.core_idea: Order every elastic architectural dimension from a shared origin so that deployable models are deterministic parameter prefixes, then distribute training updates across the desired prefix pool instead of training a separate model for each budget.
method.mechanism: For each iteration, sample truncation indices from specified supports for depth, width, heads, blocks, embeddings, or functions; intersect their origin-tied parameter prefixes to form a submodel; optimize either that stochastic submodel or a summation of related submodels; share the output classifier and checkpoint; and at inference choose a prefix directly, optionally using intermediate confidence or the prefix as a speculative draft for the full model.
assumptions: Useful capacity can be arranged monotonically in origin-tied prefixes along every targeted dimension.
A chosen sampling distribution visits each deployable configuration often enough and balances conflicting shared-weight objectives.
One shared classifier is suitable across substantially different feature widths and depths.
Accuracy and compute are sufficiently ordered that a budget maps to a prefix without expensive validation-time configuration search.
Equal optimizer-step counts are an adequate fairness criterion even when epochs, submodel forwards, and data exposure differ.
Gradient interference between jointly sampled submodels and an independently trained counterpart is negligible, despite being the structural difference between them.
Stationarity of the training objective implies stationarity of each model output for the performance-bound derivation.
CIFAR-10, GLUE fine-tuning, one GSM8K/LLaMA setting, and a toy neuron-order task transfer to architecture- and task-general claims.

techniques.role: Ties every submodel to the origin of each selected architectural dimension, making truncation deterministic.
Draws depth, width, or other prefix indices from configurable supports so only part of the pool is evaluated per iteration.
Reuses parameters, classifier, and checkpoint across all nested or sorted submodels.
Optionally aggregates losses for a selected submodel and related configurations in one training step.
Accumulates stochastic submodel gradients before optimizer updates to increase participation across the pool.
Stops LLaMA decoding at an intermediate prefix when its confidence crosses a threshold.
Uses an adaptively selected intermediate LLaMA prefix to draft tokens that a fuller prefix checks.
Uses shared training to impose a preferred neuron or component importance order for later truncation.

evaluations.setting: MobileNetV2 on CIFAR-10 across 16 depth choices and 10 width choices.
evaluations.metric: Test accuracy and recovery relative to the independently trained largest model.
evaluations.result: The 160-cell grid spans near-chance tiny models through large prefixes close to the 95.45 reference; the paper reports up to 96% recovery jointly and up to 99% for width-only sorting, not at least 96% for every submodel.
evaluations.baseline: Ordinary largest-model training, with each baseline submodel classifier additionally trained for five epochs.

evaluations.setting: cPreResNet20 on CIFAR-10 at 100%, 75%, 50%, and 25% widths under InstanceNorm and BatchNorm.
evaluations.metric: Mean test accuracy over four seeds and average across widths.
evaluations.result: SortedNet-IN averages 84.55 versus 84.10 for slimmable networks and 82.76 for LCS-p; SortedNet-BN averages 63.52 versus 59.70 and 58.22, while losing some individual width comparisons.
evaluations.baseline: Slimmable Networks, Universally Slimmable Networks/LCS-p-BN, and LCS-p-IN with optimizer updates equalized.

evaluations.setting: Layer-sorted RoBERTa-base on eight GLUE tasks using prefixes from one to twelve layers.
evaluations.metric: Task metrics and row average versus untrained intermediate-layer extraction.
evaluations.result: Average across prefixes/tasks is 76.67 versus 52.86 without SortedNet; the full 12-layer prefix scores 84.16 versus 86.13, a 1.97-point loss.
evaluations.baseline: Corresponding intermediate representations of an ordinarily fine-tuned RoBERTa-base.

evaluations.setting: LLaMA-13B fine-tuned on GSM8K with layer prefixes 12 through 40.
evaluations.metric: Milliseconds per token, claimed speedup, accuracy, and speculative rejection ratio.
evaluations.result: Stochastic-loss Sorted self-speculation reaches 47.93 ms/token (2.01x) at 23.27 accuracy for layers 12:40 and 48.66 (1.98x) at 24.33 for 12:24, versus full decoding at 96.41 and 23.95; confidence exit reaches 2.09x at 20.69.
evaluations.baseline: Full autoregressive decoding, fixed-prefix speculative decoding, confidence early exit, and a separately trained summation-loss SortedNet.

evaluations.setting: Joint BERT-large/BERT-base sorting across layers, hidden width, and attention heads on GLUE.
evaluations.result: Sorted BERT-large reaches 81.98 or 83.26 versus 83.11 independently, but extracted Sorted BERT-base reaches only 66.42 or 70.03 versus 81.07 independently.
evaluations.baseline: Pretrained references, paper-setting independently fine-tuned BERT-base/large, random initialization, and direct base extraction from large.

evaluations.setting: cPreResNet20 gradient accumulation and training-time studies on CIFAR-10.
evaluations.metric: Width-averaged accuracy, optimizer calls, epochs, and seconds per epoch.
evaluations.result: With 200 updates and 200/400/600/800 epochs, accumulation 1/2/3/4 averages 80.85/82.53/83.11/83.95. At fixed 200 epochs and 200/100/66/50 updates, averages are 80.85/80.75/81.63/82.19. Post-warmup epoch timing is 49.7 +/- 2.06 seconds versus 292.7 +/- 3.17 for LCS-p; a fourfold adjustment gives 198.8.
evaluations.baseline: LCS-p and SortedNet accumulation factors 1-4 under two non-equivalent control schemes.

evaluations.setting: One-hidden-layer, ten-neuron classifier on a four-cluster synthetic two-dimensional dataset.
evaluations.metric: Accuracy of target-order and reverse-order neuron prefixes across five runs.
evaluations.result: SortedNet target order averages 89.25 versus 59.38 in reverse, while ordinary training averages 82.22 target versus 86.67 reverse.
evaluations.baseline: The same network and optimizer under ordinary training, with neuron masking evaluated in both orders.

limitations: Author-stated: applying SortedNet during BERT pretraining is left for future research; fine-tuning alone leaves the small jointly trained BERT roughly ten points behind independent BERT-base.
Author-stated: input-adaptive sample-efficient inference beyond the demonstrated confidence heuristic is left for future work.
Reviewer-identified: the abstract's universal 96% recovery claim is false for the displayed 160-model grid.
Reviewer-identified: the empirical selection workflow evaluates and ranks all candidate submodels, so the search-free claim applies only to extraction after selection.
Reviewer-identified: MobileNetV2 uses one seed, LLaMA reports no seed or uncertainty, and most comparisons lack confidence intervals or significance tests.
Reviewer-identified: the 160-model schedule scales epochs by pool size and is not compared end to end against independent training, leaving total-compute and convergence-cost claims unresolved.

Reviewer-identified: the CIFAR-10 scalability experiment uses a baseline whose classifiers receive five extra epochs while initial SortedNet cells do not; the later adjustment experiment improves SortedNet by another roughly 2%-15%, so comparison protocols differ.
Reviewer-identified: GLUE and GSM8K results do not report validation selection, exact preprocessing, full decoding settings, or raw outputs, and Table 7 omits LLaMA entirely.
Reviewer-identified: the theory models identical independent training rather than multi-objective shared training, and neither displayed bound proves contraction, convergence, or output closeness.
Reviewer-identified: there is no official public code, checkpoint, environment, training log, or result artifact, preventing reproduction and verification of implementation-specific claims.
Reviewer-identified: the study does not measure latency, memory, energy, or throughput on actual heterogeneous deployment devices, despite motivating dynamic hardware budgets.
Reviewer-identified: the LLaMA evaluation covers one 13B model and one math dataset and changes accuracy under the purported self-speculative path, unlike lossless verification methods.
failure_modes: Small prefixes receive too little representational capacity or too few useful updates and collapse toward chance accuracy.
Gradients from larger sampled submodels overwrite or redirect shared prefix weights needed by smaller submodels.
A fixed shared classifier sees incompatible intermediate feature distributions across depths and widths.
Origin-tied ordering excludes a better non-prefix combination of layers, heads, channels, or neurons.
A deployment budget maps to several prefixes, forcing validation-time evaluation despite deterministic extraction.
Gradient accumulation changes effective exposure, batch statistics, and optimizer frequency, confounding claims about stochasticity.
Intermediate LLM exits or drafts alter answer quality even when they reduce average token latency.
BatchNorm statistics become unreliable for rarely sampled subnetworks or widths.
The largest shared model loses performance because it no longer receives every optimization step.
A theoretical argument treats shared and independent objectives as identical and consequently erases the interference it needs to explain.
reusable_insights: Separate deterministic submodel extraction from architecture selection; report the number and cost of candidates evaluated for each deployment budget.
For an elastic pool, publish per-submodel sampling counts, gradient conflicts, accuracy, cost, and uncertainty rather than only a pool size or best recovery.
Match total examples, forward/backward FLOPs, optimizer updates, and wall-clock time when comparing stochastic and summed elastic objectives.
Treat the smallest, largest, and frontier submodels as distinct objectives; a mean can hide collapse at deployable low-budget points.
Lossless speculative decoding requires explicit token-distribution or output-equivalence verification, not merely similar downstream aggregate accuracy.
A shared-training theory must retain the cross-objective gradient term and prove a contraction or bounded cumulative interference under stated sampling assumptions.
Taylor bounds on performance should operate on the optimized loss or metric surrogate, state smoothness and remainder conditions, and bound absolute deviation.
Elastic-model artifacts should release the exact configuration pool, sampling distribution, checkpoint, evaluator, latency harness, raw seeds, and per-budget frontier.
open_questions: How does SortedNet compare with HydraViT, MatFormer, Flextron, and LLaMaFlex under the same backbone, initialization, data, total FLOPs, and hardware latency protocol?
Can sampling probabilities be optimized without performing the pool-wide search the framework claims to avoid?
What Pareto frontier remains after matching total training tokens and reporting all 160 submodels with multiple seeds?
Can gradient surgery, distillation, sandwich sampling, or per-prefix normalization prevent collapse of the smallest prefixes without damaging the largest?
Does the imposed component order persist under distribution shift, calibration, robustness, and out-of-domain tasks?
Can a rigorous convergence analysis bound cumulative gradient interference across sampled shared objectives and explain when prefix ordering emerges?
Can SortedNet self-speculation be made provably output-identical while retaining its reported twofold speedup?
How much of the claimed efficiency remains in compiled kernels on edge CPUs, mobile accelerators, and batch-serving GPUs?
Will joint SortedNet pretraining close the 11-15 point BERT-base gap, and at what additional token and accelerator cost?
Can the authors release code, exact checkpoints, raw logs, and configuration-level results for independent reproduction?

competitive_landscape.title: Once-for-All: Train One Network and Specialize it for Efficient Deployment
competitive_landscape.difference: OFA progressively shrinks depth, width, kernel size, and resolution, then searches the trained supernet for hardware-specific subnetworks. SortedNet replaces progressive distillation and NAS with origin-tied stochastic prefixes, but its own best-subset demonstration still evaluates the pool.

competitive_landscape.title: DynaBERT: Dynamic BERT with Adaptive Width and Depth
competitive_landscape.difference: DynaBERT jointly adapts BERT width and depth using teacher distillation and importance-based rewiring, with public code. SortedNet offers a simpler architecture-general prefix objective, yet its own BERT-base extraction remains far below independent fine-tuning.

competitive_landscape.title: LCS: Learning Compressible Subspaces for Efficient, Adaptive, Real-Time Network Compression at Inference Time
competitive_landscape.difference: LCS learns a continuous parameter subspace supporting on-device sparsity and quantization without recalibration. SortedNet uses discrete shared prefixes and is faster per reported cPreResNet epoch, but its mean advantage under InstanceNorm is only 0.45 points over slimmable networks and its timing study is not end to end.

competitive_landscape.title: Sorted LLaMA: Unlocking the Potential of Intermediate Layers of Large Language Models for Dynamic Inference
competitive_landscape.difference: The authors' follow-up specializes sorted intermediate-layer supervision to LLaMA and develops dynamic inference in substantially more detail. It narrows, rather than independently validates, the reviewed paper's brief one-task LLaMA demonstration.

competitive_landscape.title: MatFormer: Nested Transformer for Elastic Inference
competitive_landscape.difference: MatFormer jointly trains nested FFN granularities and extracts hundreds of Mix'n'Match variants across language and vision up to 2.6B parameters. SortedNet covers more architectural axes in principle, but provides smaller-scale evidence and no public artifact; MatFormer also exposes that heuristic or NAS selection remains distinct from nested training.

competitive_landscape.title: Flextron: Many-in-One Flexible Large Language Model
competitive_landscape.difference: Flextron transforms pretrained GPT-3 and Llama-2 models into nested elastic LLMs using 7.63% of original pretraining tokens and learns input-adaptive routing to latency/accuracy targets. SortedNet is simpler and earlier but evaluates one LLaMA-13B task without a trained router or matched large-scale language frontier.

competitive_landscape.title: Draft & Verify: Lossless Large Language Model Acceleration via Self-Speculative Decoding
competitive_landscape.difference: Draft & Verify skips intermediate LLaMA-2 layers for drafting, verifies with the unchanged model, requires no training or extra memory, guarantees identical output, and reports up to 1.99x speedup. SortedNet reports a similar peak speed but requires training and its aggregate GSM8K accuracy changes from full decoding.

competitive_landscape.title: HydraViT: Stacking Heads for a Scalable ViT
competitive_landscape.difference: HydraViT varies embedding width and attention-head count and directly benchmarks SortedNet on ImageNet-1K, reporting up to five percentage points higher accuracy at equal GMACs and seven at equal throughput across ten subnetworks. This is the clearest later primary evidence against SortedNet's broad empirical-superiority framing.

competitive_landscape.title: LLaMaFlex: Many-in-one LLMs via Generalized Pruning and Weight Sharing
competitive_landscape.difference: LLaMaFlex starts from Llama 3.1 8B, performs about 60B tokens of elastic continuation, and learns a Gumbel-Softmax router that yields width/depth-pruned variants from 1B to 8B without per-variant tuning. It supplies modern LLM scale and automatic budget routing absent from SortedNet, though at substantial post-training cost.

competitive_landscape.title: ThinkingViT: Matryoshka Thinking Vision Transformer for Elastic Inference
competitive_landscape.difference: ThinkingViT progressively activates attention heads per image and recycles earlier features, directly comparing against SortedNet, MatFormer, and HydraViT on ImageNet-1K. Version 3 reports gains up to 2.0 points at equal throughput and 2.9 at equal GMACs over nested baselines, adding input adaptivity that SortedNet only proposes as future work.

competitive_landscape.title: Star Elastic: Many-in-One Reasoning LLMs with Efficient Budget Control
competitive_landscape.difference: Star Elastic adds routed nested SSM, embedding, MoE, and FFN submodels to Nemotron Nano reasoning models in one 160B-token post-training run and varies submodels across thinking and answering phases. As a 2026 preprint it is not peer-reviewed, but it extends the many-in-one idea to hybrid 30B-class reasoning models and phase-adaptive budgets far beyond SortedNet's GSM8K study.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims the first generalized, scalable, architecture-agnostic, search-free many-in-one training framework across multiple dimensions, with negligible overhead, competitive main and submodel accuracy, theoretical justification, 160 simultaneously trained models, and approximately twofold LLaMA decoding acceleration.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The origin-tied multidimensional prefix definition and stochastic-versus-summation update abstraction unify several elastic-network patterns in a compact framework. The paper spans CNNs, encoder Transformers, a decoder LLM, 160 MobileNet configurations, four-width comparisons, multi-axis BERT extraction, and a toy order-dependency check. However, slimmable networks, OFA, DynaBERT, LCS, and contemporaneous MatFormer already established many-in-one width/depth or elastic training, and the strongest headline qualifiers are not supported by the displayed results.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The defensible novelty is a simple generalized prefix parameterization with stochastic accumulation applied unusually broadly in one paper, plus an early trained self-drafting demonstration. It is not a demonstrated search-free, negligible-overhead, uniformly high-quality solution: its best-submodel workflow evaluates the whole pool, the 160-model schedule scales with pool size, many prefixes fail badly, the BERT-base gap is large, and both theoretical arguments are invalid for the stated conclusion. Later direct competitors outperform SortedNet in vision or add stronger routing, LLM-scale, and lossless-decoding evidence. With no artifact and incomplete LLaMA specification, the work is a promising framework study rather than a reproducible state-of-the-art result.

reviewer_notes: Audited the exact cached arXiv v3 PDF and extracted text: PDF/text SHA-256 values match the fulltext index, all 20 pages have usable text, and every page was rasterized and visually inspected at full-page resolution, with dense result pages rechecked individually. Reconciled Figures 1-7; Tables 1-9; Equations 1-3 and every Appendix B derivation; the full main text, related-work appendix, hyperparameters, accumulation/timing studies, classifier adjustment, BERT multi-axis study, and neuron-order experiment. Recomputed Table 2 and Table 3 means/differences, Table 4 speed-quality comparisons, Tables 5-6 update/epoch contrasts, the 160-model schedule, and the BERT gaps. The manuscript contains no artifact URL; exact title, arXiv-ID, and method/author repository searches found no official implementation through 2026-08-24. Current competitors were checked only against primary arXiv, OpenReview, ACL Anthology, CVF, PMLR, ICLR, or NeurIPS records. No shared generated data were rebuilt, and the only repository change is this absent reading.

verification.passage_check: Secondary pass reconciled every material statement against the exact text and page renderings, checked all 20/20 pages and all displayed visuals/tables/equations/appendices, recomputed headline comparisons, traced both theoretical derivations line by line, and repeated artifact-availability searches.
verification.competitor_check: Primary-source comparison completed through 2026-08-24 across direct predecessors, contemporaneous nested Transformers, later direct ImageNet benchmarks, large-scale elastic LLMs, lossless self-speculative decoding, input-adaptive vision, and 2026 reasoning-model work; peer-reviewed and preprint evidence are explicitly distinguished.
